source.title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement

record.tranche_reason: The study uses the refusal direction as a target for its own multilingual jailbreak method and reports that method’s performance. It does not isolate the causal effect of suppressing the direction, apply the original ablation/addition intervention, or test training against ablation.
record.gate_note: STEER chooses translations to lower a refusal-direction projection and reports jailbreak outcomes. These results show how the direction-guided attack performs, not whether suppressing the direction itself causes the attack to succeed. The paper also reports refusal-score distributions by response class; these are correlational, not a causal test. Table 1’s HarmBench and AdvBench values are not assigned to models because the flattened layout does not unambiguously map them. Comparative CSRT/GCG results are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: STEER uses the Arditi difference-in-means direction as an optimisation target for a code-switching jailbreak and mainly reports its own attack success rates. It applies no ablation or addition of the direction, no weight edit, no multi-direction comparison, no harm-versus-refusal separation, no direction-transfer test and no training comparison. The only direction-level result (§4.4) is a correlation between projection and refusal on prompts chosen to minimise that projection. It is not an independent test of V1 or V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction: the single-direction encoding is assumed from Arditi et al., not tested. The authors conclude that STEER exploits the refusal direction via targeted low-resource-language substitutions. They overclaim that §4.4 shows the projection is 'the actual decision variable' and that the structure generalises across six models. They frame safety as an epistemic coverage problem needing multilingual training and abstention.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of ablating or adding the original mean-difference direction, STEER uses a direction identified at a selected layer to score words and guide iterative multilingual substitutions. The paper describes this as an attack using the finding.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with paraphrase preprocessing; the authors report losses of 19 to 44 percentage points without it. Layer selection and language-pool size also change reported attack success (Tables 3 and 4; not extracted as rows).

fits_no_version.finding: A word-substitution attack guided by the refusal direction reaches 80–93% ASR@8 on JBB across six 7–9B instruct models. Paraphrase preprocessing adds 3–50 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction-guided multilingual code-switching jailbreaks open 7–9B instruct models more efficiently than random code-switching or GCG.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama-3-8B JBB attack iterations, refused responses have mean projection +3.6 and non-refused −1.2 (KS D=0.766).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projection onto the difference-in-means direction separates refused from non-refused outputs under code-switching attack.

fits_no_version.finding: STEER prompts crafted on open models transfer to GPT-4o(-mini) at 31.5–43.2% ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Direction-guided code-switched prompts partly transfer to closed models.

record.peer_reviewed: 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning (EIML@ICML 2026)
record.problems: No direct causal ablation/addition test or capability-preservation assessment. The paper notes evaluation is limited to the 7–9B range and uses an automated GPT-4o judge, which may diverge from human assessments on borderline cases. The refusal-score association is not an intervention. Results in Table 1 for HarmBench and AdvBench are not mapped to individual models because the supplied flattened layout is ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 layer-selection and Table 4 language-pool ablations are omitted; they report STEER design-choice performance rather than isolate the refusal-direction claim. Table 1 HarmBench and AdvBench model-level values are omitted because the flattened layout does not unambiguously assign values to models. CSRT/GCG comparisons are not extracted as separate rows.

untested.parts: No directional ablation, no activation addition, no capability evaluation.
No measurement of whether existing jailbreaks (GCG, CSRT) suppress the direction. No adversarial training against ablation. STEER minimises the projection by design.
No comparison of one direction against affine, cone or multi-direction accounts.
The direction is computed per model. Its cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer is not tested; only prompts transfer.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill is only an attack target; there is no reasoning-specific direction analysis.

missing.what: Per-layer Fisher ratio curves of projection separability peak sharply at a middle layer (Llama-3-8B layer 17, GLM-4-9B layer 24). This is a descriptive localisation, not a causal test.

record.verdict_notes: Workshop paper with one author. The causal language in §4.4 and §4.5 rests only on correlation and on attack success; no intervention on the direction is performed. Tables are internally inconsistent (Llama JBB 83 vs 78), and the transfer target is named inconsistently (GPT-4o vs GPT-4o-mini). A GPT-4o judge is used. I agree with the record that no version receives a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No causal ablation or addition of the direction, no test of removal across every layer and position, and no general-capability evaluation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
The study builds an attack around minimizing the refusal score, but does not isolate whether direction suppression causes attack success; it does not train against ablation.
No test comparing a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Prompt transfer to another model is reported, but transfer of the direction itself across languages, variants, or training stages is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B is evaluated as an attack target, but reasoning-specific behavior or the V1 causal claim is not tested.
